body:
> A mobile project that needs to distribute debug exports on Google Play.

I don't understand what this PR is addressing, what does it mean to distribute debug exports?

The only things the changes in this PR seem to do is swap which keystore is used to sign the builds, which you can already do by directly specifying the keystore properties in the export settings.

I'm not quite clear on the purpose of exporting a debug app without the `debuggable` attribute. If your goal is to distribute the app for internal testing, there are other more suitable methods than Google Play.

> I don't understand what this PR is addressing, what does it mean to distribute debug exports?

I'm referring to exporting a build with the "Export With Debug" toggle enabled in the file dialog that shows up when you press the "Export Project..." button.

Debug builds in Godot bring with them a slew of useful error checks (through the `DEBUG_ENABLED` macro) that we want included in internal testing builds, which are to be distributed through Google Play Console. Frankly, there is a high likelihood that this game will end up distributing debug exports for the final release even, as many of these debug checks (and upcoming features like the GDScript backtraces in #91006) are important for a live service title like this one.

However, if you try to upload one of these debug builds to Google Play Console you will be met with a rather cryptic error saying "All uploaded bundles must be signed", which as far as I can tell has nothing to do with signing, unless there's some kind of signing entitlement that I've missed. Searching around for this error will tell you that disabling the [`debuggable`](https://developer.android.com/privacy-and-security/risks/android-debuggable) attribute (either by modifying the `debug` build type or by using the `release` build type like in this PR) resolves the error, which seems to be the case. From what I've gathered Google simply does not allow you distribute builds (internally or otherwise) that have this attribute enabled, for security purposes.

It's of course possible for this PR to take the approach of adding some kind of "For Distribution" checkbox instead (which I believe is how Unreal phrases it) and then pass some custom argument along with the Gradle invocation that disables the `debuggable` attribute for Gradle's `debug` build type, but that leaves out other distribution-related features like various minifications that Gradle does for release builds.

> The only things the changes in this PR seem to do is swap which keystore is used to sign the builds, which you can already do by directly specifying the keystore properties in the export settings.

The actual important change is above the keystore changes, which changes `build_type` to read from these new export settings rather than be picked based on the value of `p_debug`.

The keystore changes are admittedly messier than they probably should have been, but what it does is change it so that the appropriate `[debug|release]_keystore_file` (etc.) is used based on what Gradle build type is desired, instead of basing it on `p_debug`. If I'd left the code as-is then you would always pass `debug_keystore_file` (etc.) when doing a debug export, which always maps to the `debug` Gradle build type, and thus wouldn't apply when using the `release` build type, resulting in an error about missing keystore.

> I'm not quite clear on the purpose of exporting a debug app without the `debuggable` attribute.

The "debug" terminology is somewhat broad/ambiguous in general, and many of the meanings are largely orthogonal to eachother. I would argue that the way Android refers to "debuggable" in the case of this attribute (which as I understand just allows you to attach a JDWP debugger) maps better to what Godot refers to as a "development build" (`dev_build=yes`), meaning one where you'd typically want to attach a debugger. Many of the things that Godot's `DEBUG_ENABLED` builds allow for are still useful even when not attaching a debugger of any kind.

> If your goal is to distribute the app for internal testing, there are other more suitable methods than Google Play.

I am admittedly somewhat new to the modern Android ecosystem, but I can't really see the argument for not wanting to lessen the friction with the first-party tools of the biggest distribution platform.

I'm still not sure about this approach. A logging system might be more suitable and Godot also generate logs on crash.

BTW Wouldn't adding the release keystore info to the "debug keystore" columns in export settings work?

> I'm still not sure about this approach. A logging system might be more suitable and Godot also generate logs on crash.

I'm not sure how this applies to this particular use-case. There is no substitute for the many error checks (and general development features) that get compiled out completely from a `DEBUG_ENABLED` build within Godot itself. I'm not strictly talking about `DEBUG_ENABLED` stuff in the project itself.

> BTW Wouldn't adding the release keystore info to the "debug keystore" columns in export settings work?

No, as mentioned in my previous comment, if I had left the keystore code as-is then you would always end up passing the `debug_keystore_[file|alias|password]` attribute to Gradle when doing a debug export from Godot, which will only ever apply to the `debug` Gradle build type, which as of this PR isn't necessarily the Gradle build type used.

> However, if you try to upload one of these debug builds to Google Play Console you will be met with a rather cryptic error saying "All uploaded bundles must be signed", which as far as I can tell has nothing to do with signing, unless there's some kind of signing entitlement that I've missed.

This is likely because your debug build is signed with a debug keystore and not a release keystore. The playstore doesn't accept debug keystore (keystores with the default credentials), so the solution here as @syntaxerror247 mentioned is to update your export options so that the debug keystore settings match the release keystore.

> Debug builds in Godot bring with them a slew of useful error checks (through the DEBUG_ENABLED macro) that we want included in internal testing builds

There's a misunderstanding about how the Android gradle build system works; the build type that's passed to the gradle build is used [here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/fd4c29a189e53a1e085df5b9b9a05cac9351b3ef/platform/android/java/app/build.gradle#L47-L49) to select which **prebuilt** Godot Android library is used.
So your changes are effectively a no-op; by selecting 'Export with debug' but setting the build type to `Release`, you're pretty much doing a normal release build. The release version of the Godot Android library will be used and the `DEBUG_ENABLED` macro will be false.

> I would argue that the way Android refers to "debuggable" in the case of this attribute (which as I understand just allows you to attach a JDWP debugger) maps better to what Godot refers to as a "development build" (dev_build=yes)

I don't disagree with that; in fact this is the [approach used for the Godot Android editor](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/fd4c29a189e53a1e085df5b9b9a05cac9351b3ef/platform/android/java/editor/build.gradle#L127-L132). 
However unlike the Android editor, regular users don't get the option for a `dev` build, so setting `debuggable` to `false` for `debug` builds mean they also lose the ability to use certain tools that require that setting to properly operate.

Though, it's a discussion worth having whether we should provide additional options in order to customize that behavior.
In the meantime, to unblock yourself you can grab the `godot-lib.template_debug.aar` from `res://android/build/build/libs/debug` and copy it to the `res://android/build/build/libs/release` folder (make sure you also delete `godot-lib.template_release.aar` from that folder).
This will give you what you were looking for; i.e: generate a release Android apk that uses the debug version of the Godot Android library.

> Though, it's a discussion worth having whether we should provide additional options in order to customize that behavior.

@mihe One option would be to add an advanced setting `gradle_debuggable` with the following values:
- `auto`: set `debuggable` to `true` for `debug` builds and `false` for `release` builds
- `true`: `debuggable` is always `true`
- `false`: `debuggable` is always `false`

> One option would be to add an advanced setting gradle_debuggable with the following values

I was also thinking about this solution, though I was considering using a boolean instead. But enum should be better.

Implementing it would be also pretty simple, just add a check at the time of [manifest creation](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/fd4c29a189e53a1e085df5b9b9a05cac9351b3ef/platform/android/export/gradle_export_util.cpp#L308) and handle `android:debuggable` value conditionally.

EDIT: But I am still not sure that we need this export setting though (even after reading these long comments). It seems like a niche use case that could be addressed with a custom template or manually editing manifest in gradle build. Adding DEBUG_ENABLED macro in a _release app_  also has several disadvantages
- It can cause `performance overhead` as it will do additional checks and diagnostics that are not optimized for performance.
- It also increases `binary size` by several megabytes.
- I guess, debug build also doesn't have better error handling and it can have craches.

> This is likely because your debug build is signed with a debug keystore and not a release keystore. The playstore doesn't accept debug keystore (keystores with the default credentials), so the solution here as @syntaxerror247 mentioned is to update your export options so that the debug keystore settings match the release keystore.

This was one of the first things we tried. Providing a non-debug keystore for the debug keystore settings does not resolve the error on its own. Setting the `debuggable` attribute to `false` in `res://android/build/build.gradle` (which I assume is [this](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/fd4c29a189e53a1e085df5b9b9a05cac9351b3ef/platform/android/java/app/build.gradle#L178-L187) file) did however resolve the error (while also using a non-debug keystore).

> There's a misunderstanding about how the Android gradle build system works; the build type that's passed to the gradle build is used [here](https://github.com/godotengine/godot/blob/fd4c29a189e53a1e085df5b9b9a05cac9351b3ef/platform/android/java/app/build.gradle#L47-L49) to select which **prebuilt** Godot Android library is used.
> So your changes are effectively a no-op; by selecting 'Export with debug' but setting the build type to `Release`, you're pretty much doing a normal release build. The release version of the Godot Android library will be used and the `DEBUG_ENABLED` macro will be false.

That does indeed seem to have been a misunderstanding on my part.

> However unlike the Android editor, regular users don't get the option for a `dev` build, so setting `debuggable` to `false` for `debug` builds mean they also lose the ability to use certain tools that require that setting to properly operate.

Right, yes, just to be clear, I'm not advocating for changing anything about the default state of debug exports. I just wanted to make clear that there's some ambiguity with debug/debuggable here.

> Though, it's a discussion worth having whether we should provide additional options in order to customize that behavior.
> In the meantime, to unblock yourself you can grab the `godot-lib.template_debug.aar` from `res://android/build/build/libs/debug` and copy it to the `res://android/build/build/libs/release` folder (make sure you also delete `godot-lib.template_release.aar` from that folder).

We've already unblocked ourselves by manually changing the manifest to set `debuggable` to `false`, as mentioned above, but moving these `*.aar` files around sounds more like what this pull request was trying to achieve, so I can give that a try.

> One option would be to add an advanced setting `gradle_debuggable`

I did consider taking a similar approach to this, but as mentioned previously we are also considering shipping debug exports, and from what I understand (and correct me if I'm wrong) there are other things happening as part of the Gradle `release` build type that would be appropriate for production builds, like certain types of minification?

> EDIT: But I am still not sure that we need this export setting though (even after reading these long comments). It seems like a niche use case that could be addressed with a custom template or manually editing manifest in gradle build.

Assuming that this `debuggable` attribute is in fact the culprit here then I do think `debuggable` should be configurable as an export option. While the use-case of shipping debug exports for production use is admittedly niche, the use-case of wanting debug exports for internal testing builds seems much less niche to me. Frankly I'm a bit surprised nobody else has reported this problem already.

> Adding DEBUG_ENABLED macro in a _release app_ also has several disadvantages
> 
> * It can cause `performance overhead` as it will do additional checks and diagnostics that are not optimized for performance.
> * It also increases `binary size` by several megabytes.
> * I guess, debug build also doesn't have better error handling and it can have craches.

Yes, certainly. We're aware of these trade-offs though.

---

Anyway, it's clear that this PR isn't the correct approach here, so I'll go ahead and close this.

I struggle to see the workaround of moving/picking `*.aar` files made into any sort of export option worth upstreaming, and while configuring the `debuggable` attribute definitely seems worthwhile/useful, it's unclear right now whether that's going to be enough for our purposes, so I'll hold off with making a new proposal/PR for now.
